lessonTitle: Haemostasis and Haematological Malignancy: PT, APTT, Anticoagulants and Leukaemia

blocks.text: A 5-year-old boy falls from a low wall and, over the next day, his right knee swells tense and painful with blood. His mother says his older uncle has the same problem. His platelet count is normal, his prothrombin time is normal, but his activated partial thromboplastin time is markedly prolonged. Two simple clotting tests have narrowed the fault to one limb of the coagulation cascade.

blocks.markdown: **Haemostasis** is the process that stops bleeding while keeping blood fluid in intact vessels. Primary haemostasis is the platelet plug. **Secondary haemostasis** is the coagulation cascade, in which serine protease clotting factors activate one another in sequence until soluble fibrinogen (factor I) is converted by thrombin (factor IIa) into insoluble fibrin, forming a stable clot. Most clotting factors are made in the liver.

### Extrinsic, intrinsic and common pathways

The **extrinsic pathway** begins when tissue factor, exposed at the site of vessel injury, binds **factor VII**. The **intrinsic pathway** involves factors **XII, XI, IX and VIII** and is activated by contact with negatively charged surfaces. Both converge on the **common pathway**: factor **X** (with factor V) activates prothrombin (II) to thrombin, which converts fibrinogen to fibrin. In the laboratory the two pathways are tested separately.

blocks.caption: Interpreting PT and APTT together

blocks.title: Locating the factor deficiency from PT and APTT
blocks.prompt: A 22-year-old man has prolonged bleeding after a tooth extraction. His platelet count is normal, PT is 12 s (normal), and APTT is 62 s (reference about 25-35 s). A mixing study with normal plasma corrects the APTT. Which pathway is affected?

steps.text: A normal PT means the extrinsic and common pathways are working, so factors VII, X, V, II and fibrinogen are sufficient.
A prolonged APTT places the defect in the intrinsic pathway: factors XII, XI, IX or VIII.

Correction with normal plasma shows a factor deficiency rather than an inhibitor. Specific factor assays would then identify VIII or IX; a bleeding disorder with tooth-extraction bleeding in a male suggests haemophilia (X-linked).

blocks.answer: The intrinsic pathway, most likely a deficiency of factor VIII or IX (haemophilia).

blocks.markdown:
### Warfarin and the direct oral anticoagulants

**Warfarin** inhibits the enzyme vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1), preventing recycling of vitamin K. Without active vitamin K, the liver cannot carry out gamma-carboxylation of factors **II, VII, IX and X** and of the anticoagulant proteins **C and S**, so they are made in inactive form. Its effect is slow because circulating factors must decay first, and it is monitored by the PT, reported as the **INR**. Protein C and factor VII have the shortest half-lives, so in the first days warfarin can transiently favour clotting. **Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs)** act directly on one clotting enzyme: **rivaroxaban and apixaban inhibit factor Xa**, and **dabigatran inhibits thrombin (factor IIa)**. They act within hours, have predictable effects and do not require routine INR monitoring.

blocks.caption: International normalised ratio. ISI = international sensitivity index of the thromboplastin reagent (about 1.0 for modern reagents).

blocks.title: Calculating an INR
blocks.prompt: A patient on warfarin has a PT of 30 s. The mean normal PT is 12 s and the ISI is 1.0. Calculate the INR.

steps.text: Raise to the power of ISI: 2.5^1.0 = 2.5.
A common therapeutic target for many indications is 2.0-3.0, so this is within it. Targets vary with indication.

rows: VKORC1; reduces functional II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S
Direct inhibition of factor Xa (rivaroxaban, apixaban) or thrombin (dabigatran)
Specific antidotes or prothrombin complex concentrate

blocks.markdown:
### Leukaemia: acute versus chronic

**Leukaemias** are malignancies of haematopoietic cells that arise in the marrow. They are divided by **maturity** of the cell and by **tempo**. **Acute leukaemia** is a clonal proliferation of immature **blasts** (at least 20% blasts in marrow, by common criteria) that block normal maturation, so marrow failure appears within weeks: anaemia, neutropenia with infection and thrombocytopenia with bleeding. **Chronic leukaemia** involves proliferation of relatively mature cells that accumulate over months to years and may be discovered incidentally on a blood count.

rows: Marrow failure; DIC in the promyelocytic form
Mature granulocytes at all stages; Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22), BCR-ABL fusion
Splenomegaly, raised white count, insidious onset
Mature-appearing small B lymphocytes; smudge cells
blocks.caption: Main leukaemia types

points: PT tests the extrinsic and common pathways (factor VII) and APTT the intrinsic and common pathways (factors XII, XI, IX, VIII), so the pattern of prolongation localises the defect.

Warfarin inhibits vitamin K-dependent carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S and is monitored by INR, whereas DOACs directly inhibit factor Xa or thrombin and act rapidly without routine monitoring.

Acute leukaemias are rapid proliferations of immature blasts causing marrow failure, whereas chronic leukaemias are slow expansions of mature cells, with CML defined by BCR-ABL and CLL by small mature B cells.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman has a pre-operative coagulation screen showing a normal PT and a markedly prolonged APTT, and is taking no anticoagulant. Which pathway is affected?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a prolonged APTT with a normal PT localises the defect to factors VIII, IX, XI or XII.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: an extrinsic defect would prolong the PT.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: a common pathway defect would prolong both tests.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: platelet defects give normal clotting tests.

questions.explanation: The APTT assesses the intrinsic and common pathways, and a normal PT shows the common and extrinsic pathways are intact. Factor VIII, IX, XI or XII deficiency would give this pattern.

questions.stem: A patient who started warfarin 36 hours ago has a prolonged PT and a normal APTT. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Early fall in factor VII, which has the shortest half-life of the vitamin K-dependent factors

questions.correctOptionText: Early fall in factor VII, which has the shortest half-life of the vitamin K-dependent factors

distractorRationale.a: Correct: factor VII falls first and is tested by the PT, so the extrinsic pathway is the first affected.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: factor VIII is not vitamin K dependent and affects the APTT.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: excess fibrinogen does not prolong the PT.

questions.explanation: Factor VII has a half-life of only a few hours, so it falls first after warfarin starts, prolonging the PT while the APTT remains normal. As factors II, IX and X decline later, the APTT also prolongs.

questions.stem: What is the principal mechanism of action of warfarin?

options.text: Inhibition of vitamin K epoxide reductase, reducing carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX and X

questions.correctOptionText: Inhibition of vitamin K epoxide reductase, reducing carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX and X

distractorRationale.a: Correct: warfarin blocks vitamin K recycling, so these factors are made without functional gamma-carboxyl groups.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this is the mechanism of rivaroxaban and apixaban.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this is the mechanism of heparin.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this is the mechanism of dabigatran.

questions.explanation: Warfarin is a vitamin K antagonist. Factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C and S) need vitamin K-dependent carboxylation to bind calcium and phospholipid surfaces, so their activity falls.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old man with atrial fibrillation is switched from warfarin to apixaban. Which statement about apixaban is correct?

options.text: It directly inhibits factor Xa and does not need routine INR monitoring
It inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase and needs INR monitoring
It directly inhibits thrombin and acts only after several days
It activates antithrombin and is monitored by the APTT

questions.correctOptionText: It directly inhibits factor Xa and does not need routine INR monitoring

distractorRationale.a: Correct: apixaban is a direct factor Xa inhibitor with predictable pharmacology.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: thrombin inhibition is dabigatran, and DOACs act within hours.

questions.explanation: Direct oral anticoagulants target a single clotting enzyme, either factor Xa or thrombin. Their effect is predictable, so routine laboratory monitoring is not needed.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old has pallor, bruising and fever for three weeks. The blood film shows many lymphoid blasts, and bone marrow shows 80% blasts. Which diagnosis fits best?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a child with rapid-onset marrow failure and a marrow full of lymphoid blasts has ALL.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: CLL affects older adults and consists of mature small lymphocytes.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: CML is a chronic disease of adults with maturing granulocytes.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: iron deficiency does not produce blasts.

questions.explanation: A short history with anaemia, bruising from thrombocytopenia and fever from neutropenia, together with immature cells above the 20% threshold, defines acute leukaemia. Lymphoid lineage in childhood indicates ALL.

questions.stem: A patient on warfarin has a PT of 27 s, the laboratory's mean normal PT is 13.5 s and the reagent ISI is 1.1. Calculate the INR, using INR = (PT patient / mean normal PT)^ISI.
questions.explanation: The PT ratio is 27 / 13.5 = 2.0, and raising to the power 1.1 gives 2^1.1 = 2.14. This is within a commonly used target range of 2.0-3.0.

questions.stem: In a bone marrow aspirate, 300 nucleated cells are counted and 78 are blasts. Calculate the blast percentage.
questions.explanation: Blast percentage is 78 / 300 x 100 = 26%. This is above the 20% threshold commonly used to define acute leukaemia, in a clinical context with marrow failure.

questions.stem: Explain what the PT and APTT measure and how their pattern localises a coagulation defect. Give an example for each of the four possible patterns.
markingGuide: PT: extrinsic (factor VII) and common pathway; APTT: intrinsic (XII, XI, IX, VIII) and common pathway
Normal PT with prolonged APTT: intrinsic defect, for example haemophilia A or B
Prolonged PT with normal APTT: factor VII, for example early warfarin or vitamin K deficiency
Both prolonged: common pathway or multiple factors, for example liver failure, DIC, heavy warfarin
Both normal: platelet or vascular disorder, for example immune thrombocytopenia
questions.explanation: The two tests are the readouts of overlapping cascades, so comparing them identifies the likely region. This guides further factor assays.

questions.stem: Compare the mechanisms of action of warfarin and the direct oral anticoagulants, including monitoring and onset. Explain why warfarin takes days to reach full effect and why it may transiently promote clotting when first started.
markingGuide: Warfarin inhibits VKORC1, reducing functional factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S
DOACs directly inhibit factor Xa (rivaroxaban, apixaban) or thrombin (dabigatran)
Warfarin monitored by INR; DOACs do not need routine monitoring
Delay: existing functional factors must be cleared according to their half-lives; factor II has the longest half-life
Protein C and factor VII have short half-lives, so anticoagulant protein C falls early and may temporarily favour clotting
questions.explanation: Warfarin only stops new synthesis of functional factors, so anticoagulation lags while existing factors decay. Because the natural anticoagulant protein C falls before the long-lived procoagulant factors, a transient prothrombotic state can occur.

questions.stem: Differentiate acute from chronic leukaemia in terms of cell maturity and tempo, and describe how CML and CLL differ.
markingGuide: Acute: immature blasts (20% or more in marrow), arrested maturation, rapid onset over weeks
Acute: marrow failure with anaemia, neutropenic infection, thrombocytopenic bleeding
Chronic: relatively mature cells accumulating over months to years, often incidental
CML: myeloid lineage, Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) BCR-ABL, splenomegaly, middle age
CLL: mature small B lymphocytes, smudge cells, lymphocytosis, older adults
questions.explanation: Acute leukaemias are defined by arrest of cells at an immature stage, so normal cells are crowded out quickly. Chronic leukaemias retain maturation, so cell counts rise gradually and symptoms are slower to appear.
